school_choice.explainer: Traditional public schools are run by local school districts and are free and open to all students. Charter schools are also free public schools funded by tax dollars, but they're run independently — usually by a nonprofit under a contract (a 'charter') — with more freedom over how they teach and hire, and less district oversight. Private schools charge tuition and don't receive state funding. 'School choice' also sometimes means vouchers — public money families could put toward private-school tuition — which California does not currently offer.
school_choice.current_policy: California has about 1,283 charter schools, plus seven districts made up entirely of charters (state data, May 2024). They teach roughly 11.7% of public-school students. Two 2019 laws — [AB 1505](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1505) and [AB 1507](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1507), both signed that October and effective July 1, 2020 — made it harder to open and renew charters. Districts can now turn down a new charter by pointing to the financial hit or community impact, charters generally can't run campuses outside the district that approved them, and a low-performing charter can be denied renewal. California offers no state-funded private-school vouchers or education savings accounts. (A voucher gives families public money to spend on private-school tuition; an education savings account, or ESA, is a government-funded account parents can spend on tuition, tutoring, or other approved education costs.) The last voucher measure, [Prop 38](https://www.lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/38_11_2000.html) in 2000, lost 71% to 29%.
key_facts: About 1,283 charter schools and 7 all-charter districts were operating in California (state data, May 2024); charters teach roughly 11.7% of public-school students (2022-23).

[AB 1505](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1505) (2019) ended the old near-automatic right to appeal a rejected charter, and let districts cite the financial hit and community need when turning down or refusing to renew one.

[AB 1507](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1507) (2019) stopped most new charters from running learning centers or satellite campuses outside the district that approved them (the 'charter authorizer' — the agency, usually a school district, that grants and oversees the charter).
Charter enrollment has ticked up while regular district enrollment has fallen, partly because total statewide enrollment is dropping.

[Prop 38](https://www.lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/38_11_2000.html) (2000), which would have given families a voucher of about $4,000 per child, lost 71% to 29%. No statewide voucher has reached the ballot since.
school_choice.comparison: California is one of the stricter big states on school choice: it has a large charter sector but, unlike Arizona, Florida, or Indiana, offers no private-school vouchers or education savings accounts. Its 2019 laws cut against the national trend, which has been toward expanding private-school choice.
school_choice.arguments_for_change: People who want more choice say charters give families — disproportionately lower-income families and families of color — an option besides their assigned neighborhood school, and that some charter networks get strong results for those students. They argue [AB 1505](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=201920200AB1505) gave districts a money-based reason to block competitors, and that vouchers or education savings accounts would open up choice to families who can't afford private tuition or a move into a top-rated school zone.
school_choice.arguments_against_change: Opponents — including the California Teachers Association (CTA) and the California School Boards Association (CSBA) — say charters and vouchers pull per-pupil dollars (the funding that follows each student) away from district schools, which still teach most kids and still have fixed bills to pay. They argue charter quality is uneven and oversight is weaker, point to research (such as Stanford's CREDO studies) showing charter results vary a lot by operator and state, and note that California voters have repeatedly rejected vouchers as using public money to pay for private and religious schools.

school_funding.explainer: A few terms come up a lot here. 'Prop 98' is a 1988 amendment to the state constitution that sets a yearly minimum the state must spend on K-12 schools and community colleges. 'LCFF,' the Local Control Funding Formula, is the 2013 system for handing out that money: every district gets a base amount per student, plus extra for students who are low-income, learning English, or in foster care. 'Per-pupil spending' is total school money divided by the number of students. 'NAEP' is a national test (nicknamed 'the Nation's Report Card') that lets you compare states. A 'parcel tax' is a flat local tax on each property that some districts use to raise extra school money.
school_funding.current_policy: K-12 funding rests on two pillars. [Prop 98](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4929) (1988) is a constitutional rule that sets a yearly minimum the state must spend on schools and community colleges. The Local Control Funding Formula (LCFF, 2013) decides how that money is split: every district gets a base grant per student, plus a supplemental grant (an extra 20% of the base) and, for districts with lots of high-need students, a concentration grant — all aimed at students who are low-income, learning English, or in foster care. For 2024-25, the Prop 98 minimum was about $115.3 billion total (roughly $101.1 billion for K-12). Voters also passed [Prop 2](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2024) in November 2024, a $10 billion bond to build and fix school and community-college buildings.
key_facts: Total spending per student from all sources was about $23,878 for 2024-25 (state estimate), and is projected to keep rising.
On apples-to-apples Census figures, California spent about $19,894 per student in 2022-23 — roughly 13th among the states, up from 28th the year before.
LCFF (2013) stacks a supplemental grant (an extra 20% of the base) and a concentration grant on top of each district's base grant to steer more money to higher-need districts.

On the 2024 NAEP national test, California scored just below the national average — for example, 4th-grade reading 212 vs. 214 and 8th-grade reading 254 vs. 257 — though its long-run gap with the rest of the country has narrowed.

[Prop 2](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=2&year=2024) (November 2024) authorized $10 billion in bonds for K-12 and community-college buildings; many districts also charge local parcel taxes (a flat tax on each property), which need two-thirds voter approval.
school_funding.comparison: Once you adjust for California's high costs, its per-student spending now sits in the upper-middle of the states, though still below big spenders like New York. Its NAEP scores still come in below the national average, which keeps the debate alive over whether the problem is too few dollars, how the dollars get spent, or a lack of accountability.
school_funding.arguments_for_change: People who want more funding and stronger local control say California still spends less per student than comparable high-cost states, and that LCFF's supplemental and concentration grants should be bigger to close opportunity gaps for low-income students, English learners, and foster youth. They argue a steady, dedicated source of money — a tax or a bond — is needed for competitive teacher pay, school buildings, and expanding transitional kindergarten, and that local educators, not Sacramento mandates, know best how to spend it.
school_funding.arguments_against_change: People who stress accountability and reform say spending has climbed a lot since LCFF without matching gains on NAEP, so the priority should be showing where the concentration-grant money actually goes and getting measurable results — not new taxes. They note that [Prop 98](https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4929) already guarantees a rising floor, that the state budget swings with the economy, and that LCFF's loose spending rules make it hard to confirm the extra money is reaching the high-need students it's meant for.
